8.text:
## Background
Paul the apostle wrote Romans around AD 57 from Corinth, before taking a collection to Jerusalem. He had not yet visited the church in Rome, a mix of Jewish and Gentile believers, so he set out the gospel carefully: God's righteousness given through faith to all. Chapter 8 follows Paul's honest description in chapter 7 of wanting to do good yet being defeated by sin. Here he answers that struggle with the work of God's Spirit, and many readers consider it the high point of the letter.

## What happens
Paul opens with a verdict: there is "no condemnation" for those in Christ Jesus (v. 1). The law could show what is right but could not make weak human beings do it. God did what the law could not by sending his Son, who dealt with sin in human flesh, so that the law's righteous aim is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit (vv. 2–4).

Paul then contrasts two ways of living. A mind set on the flesh leads to death and hostility toward God. A mind set on the Spirit brings life and peace (vv. 5–8). The Spirit dwells in believers, and the same Spirit who raised Jesus will one day give life to their mortal bodies (vv. 9–11). So they owe the flesh nothing. By the Spirit they "put to death" sinful deeds (vv. 12–13).

Those led by the Spirit are God's children. They have not received a spirit of fear but of adoption, and they call God "Abba, Father" (vv. 14–16). Children are heirs with Christ, sharing his sufferings now and his glory later (v. 17).

Paul says present sufferings cannot compare with coming glory (v. 18). All creation, subjected to frustration and decay, groans like a woman in labor, waiting to be set free along with God's children (vv. 19–22). Believers groan too as they wait for the redemption of their bodies, and they hope for what they cannot yet see (vv. 23–25). Even when they do not know how to pray, the Spirit intercedes for them with wordless groans (vv. 26–27).

God works all things together for good for those who love him (v. 28). Paul traces God's purpose from foreknowing to glorifying (vv. 29–30). Then he asks: if God is for us, who can be against us (v. 31)? God gave his own Son, Christ intercedes, and no accusation stands (vv. 32–34). Hardship, persecution and even death, which Paul describes by quoting Psalm 44:22, cannot separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus (vv. 35–39).

## Key words and ideas
- Flesh and Spirit: "flesh" here does not mean the body as bad. It means human life turned away from God and relying on itself. "Spirit" is God's own presence living in believers.
- Adoption: in Roman law an adopted son gained full rights as heir. "Abba" is the Aramaic word for father that Jesus himself used. It is warm and personal.
- Groaning: creation, believers and the Spirit all groan (vv. 22, 23, 26). Paul treats longing and pain as part of the life of faith, a sign of birth rather than of abandonment.
- Foreknew and predestined (vv. 29–30): Christians read these words differently. Reformed Protestants see God's sovereign choice of particular people. Many Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist and other readers stress that God's foreknowledge includes human free response, or read the passage as being about the church as a whole. All agree that it is meant to comfort believers with God's faithful purpose.

## Connections
John 3:18–19 likewise says that whoever believes is not condemned. Genesis 50:20, where Joseph tells his brothers that God meant their evil for good, gives a living example of verse 28. Romans 5:3–5 earlier described suffering producing endurance and a hope that does not disappoint. Ephesians 1:4–5 also links God's choosing with adoption as children. 1 John 3:2 and Philippians 3:21 describe being made like Christ, even in our bodies, which echoes being "conformed to the image of his Son." Psalm 118:6 shares the confidence of verse 31: "The Lord is on my side; I will not fear."

## For reflection
- What would change if you truly believed there is "no condemnation" for you today?
- Where are you groaning right now, and how might the Spirit be praying with you in it?
- Which item in Paul's list (vv. 35–39) do you most fear could separate you from God's love?
